items.q: What is a bitrate ladder in a video system?

options.t: The order in which segments are downloaded
options.why: Segments are downloaded in playback order. The ladder is about which quality version you download, not the sequence.

options.t: The set of renditions of one video: several resolutions and bitrates
options.why: Right. Each rung is one encoded version; the player climbs or drops between rungs as the network changes.

options.t: The priority queue used by the transcode farm
options.why: That's the job scheduler's priority lanes. The ladder is output, not scheduling.

options.t: The CDN cache hierarchy that decides where bytes are stored, from edge to origin
options.why: That hierarchy is real but separate — it's about where bytes are stored, not what versions exist.

items.q: What is the mezzanine file, and why must it never be deleted?

options.t: The 1080p rendition, kept because it is the most-watched one and the cheapest to re-serve
options.why: The most-watched rendition is derived data — it can always be re-encoded. The mezzanine is the thing it is derived from.

options.t: The manifest that lists all renditions
options.why: That's the manifest (m3u8/mpd), a small text file that is trivially regenerated from the segments.

options.t: The original master the uploader sent
options.why: Exactly. Renditions are rebuildable; the source is not. Lose it and you can never re-encode into a new codec.

options.t: A cached copy of the video held at the edge
options.why: Edge copies are disposable by design — that's the point of a cache.

items.q: Why must the transcoder split a video into chunks only at keyframe boundaries?

options.t: To keep every chunk exactly the same number of bytes
options.why: Chunks are never equal in bytes — complex scenes compress worse. Equal size isn't a goal anywhere in this pipeline.

options.t: Frames between keyframes are stored as differences from their neighbours
options.why: Correct. A keyframe is decodable alone; everything after it references neighbours, so a cut mid-run produces garbage.

options.t: Because HTTP range requests can only address byte offsets that fall on keyframe boundaries
options.why: HTTP knows nothing about video. Range requests work on any byte offset — the constraint comes from the codec.

options.t: So the audio and video tracks stay in sync
options.why: A/V sync is handled by timestamps in the container. Keyframe cuts are about decodability.

items.q: What makes a mid-video quality switch seamless instead of a visible stutter?

options.t: Every rung has keyframes at the same timestamps
options.why: Yes — adaptive streaming is a promise made by the encoder. Aligned keyframes make the pieces swappable.

options.t: The player downloads both qualities for a moment and cross-fades between them at the switch
options.why: Nobody downloads two rungs at once — that would double bandwidth exactly when bandwidth is scarce.

options.t: The CDN re-encodes on the fly to the requested bitrate
options.why: CDNs serve static files. Transcoding at the edge would destroy cacheability and cost a fortune.

options.t: DRM keys rotate at each switch point
options.why: Key rotation is a security mechanism unrelated to how smoothly quality changes.

items.q: Where does the adaptive-bitrate decision actually get made?

options.t: At the CDN edge, based on the viewer's IP
options.why: The edge just serves files. It has no view of the player's buffer, which is the signal that matters most.

options.t: In the player
options.why: Right, and that's what lets the server stay dumb: static files, one cached copy for millions of different networks.

options.t: In the packager, when segments are written
options.why: The packager produces all rungs ahead of time; it can't know any individual viewer's conditions.

options.t: In the origin, per playback session
options.why: Per-session origin logic would defeat caching entirely, which is the whole basis of video delivery economics.

items.q: What does a streaming manifest (.m3u8 or .mpd) contain?

options.t: The encoded video data itself, base64-encoded
options.why: Manifests are tiny text files. Putting media in them would make them uncacheable and enormous.

options.t: The DRM keys needed to decrypt the stream
options.why: Keys come from a separate license server after an entitlement check — never from a publicly cacheable file.

options.t: A list of available rungs and where each rung's segments live
options.why: Correct — it's the map the player reads to know what qualities exist and which URLs to fetch next.

options.t: The viewer's playback history, so the session can resume exactly where it stopped
options.why: Resume position is per-user state in your own service; manifests are identical for everyone, which is why they cache.

items.q: What is origin shielding?

options.t: Encrypting traffic between the edge and the origin
options.why: That's transport security. Shielding is about who is allowed to talk to the origin, not about encryption.

options.t: Rate limiting playback requests per viewer
options.why: Per-viewer rate limits protect against abuse, but do nothing about thousands of edges all missing the same object.

options.t: Blocking direct downloads and hotlinking with signed URLs that expire after a few minutes
options.why: Signed URLs stop hotlinking. They don't reduce the number of upstream fetches on a cache miss.

options.t: A regional cache tier sitting between the edges and the origin
options.why: Right. The shield absorbs and consolidates misses so the origin sees a trickle instead of a stampede.

items.q: You shorten segments from 6 seconds to 2 seconds. What do you gain and lose?

options.t: Faster quality reaction and lower live latency; worse compression, more requests
options.why: Exactly the trade. Each segment starts with an expensive keyframe, so shorter segments cost bytes and request overhead.

options.t: Better compression efficiency, at the cost of a lower CDN hit rate across more objects
options.why: Backwards on compression — shorter segments compress worse because keyframes come more often.

options.t: Nothing changes except file naming
options.why: Segment length is one of the most consequential knobs in the whole system, especially for live latency.

options.t: Gain DRM strength; lose startup speed
options.why: Segment length has nothing to do with DRM, and shorter segments usually help startup, not hurt it.

items.q: In Netflix's Open Connect, what is the nightly fill window for?

options.t: Copying viewing history and logs from the appliances back to the central data center
options.why: Fill is about pushing video content outward, not pulling user data inward.

options.t: Pushing predicted-popular content onto appliances while the network is idle
options.why: Yes — it converts expensive peak-time bandwidth into nearly free off-peak bandwidth, which only works with a predictable catalog.

options.t: Re-encoding the catalog on the appliances themselves
options.why: Appliances serve bytes; encoding happens centrally where the mezzanine and the compute live.

options.t: Rotating DRM keys on cached content
options.why: Keys are served by the license service, not shipped with cached segments.

items.q: A 4-hour documentary is uploaded. One core would grind out its full H.264 ladder in about 12 hours, but your SLA says playable in 5 minutes. What's the move?

options.t: Buy a far bigger machine with many more cores and encode the whole file on that single box
options.why: A 64-core box gets you to roughly 11 minutes, at enormous cost, and still misses. Worse, the next 8-hour upload breaks the SLA all over again — one machine doesn't scale with content length.

options.t: Split at keyframes, fan (chunk x rung) tasks across workers, then stitch
options.why: Correct — and the win grows with video length, which is exactly the property you need. Watch the tail task: one stuck chunk sets your SLA.

options.t: Serve the mezzanine directly until the ladder finishes
options.why: The mezzanine is huge and in a format many devices can't play. You'd blow the viewer's bandwidth and still fail on some devices.

options.t: Encode only 360p and never build the rest
options.why: Baseline-first is right; never building the rest isn't. Popular content must earn its higher rungs, not be denied them.

items.q: An engineer proposes 2-second chunks instead of 30-second chunks, to maximize parallelism. What's the strongest objection?

options.t: Workers cannot start fast enough for 2-second tasks, so scheduling overhead dominates the run
options.why: Worker startup is a real overhead but a solvable one — warm pools exist. There's a deeper cost.

options.t: The manifest would become too large to cache
options.why: Chunk size for transcoding is independent of the segment size you publish; and manifests stay small either way.

options.t: Each chunk restarts rate control and loses lookahead, so output is permanently fatter
options.why: Right. You'd trade a one-time wall-clock win for a permanent egress cost, which is the expensive side of this system.

options.t: Keyframes can't occur every 2 seconds
options.why: They can — a 2-second keyframe interval is common. The problem is compression efficiency, not feasibility.

items.q: Your transcode dashboard shows 60,000 queued jobs. Your manager asks if that's bad. What's the right answer?

options.t: Yes — 60,000 is far above normal, so scale the fleet
options.why: Depth without context means nothing. A big fleet may be draining 60,000 jobs in two minutes.

options.t: It depends on queue age per priority lane, not depth
options.why: Right. 'The oldest fast-lane job is 14 minutes old' is actionable against the SLA; a raw count is not.

options.t: No — queues are meant to absorb bursts, so depth never matters
options.why: Half true and dangerously complacent: queues absorb bursts, but a queue that never drains is an outage in slow motion.

options.t: Yes, and the fix is to drop the oldest jobs to protect latency
options.why: Dropping uploads loses creator work for no reason — the mezzanine is safe in blob storage, so late is fine, lost is not.

items.q: A hit series drops at midnight. In the first 30 seconds, tens of thousands of edges request the same first segment, and your origin falls over. What fixes it?

options.t: Increase origin capacity 100x for launch nights
options.why: Brute force that you pay for every night for one minute of load, and it still melts on a bigger launch.

options.t: Give each edge a longer cache TTL
options.why: TTL helps after the first fetch. The stampede is precisely the moment before anyone has the object.

options.t: Shield tier plus request coalescing, and pre-position before release
options.why: Correct on both timescales: coalescing collapses simultaneous misses into one fetch, and pre-positioning means there's no miss at all.

options.t: Tell players to stagger their start with a few seconds of random delay at midnight
options.why: You cannot ask viewers to wait to watch the thing they stayed up for. Fix it in the infrastructure.

items.q: Users on stable connections complain that quality flips up and down constantly, which they hate more than steady lower quality. What's the fix?

options.t: Lock each session to the rung chosen at startup so quality never changes mid-video
options.why: That trades flapping for stalls — a network dip mid-session now means buffering instead of a graceful step down.

options.t: Use buffer occupancy as the control signal in steady state
options.why: Right. Video traffic is bursty and on-off, so throughput samples lie; a healthy buffer is direct evidence you can hold a higher rung.

options.t: Reduce the number of rungs to two
options.why: Fewer rungs means coarser adaptation — the switches get less frequent but far more jarring.

options.t: Move ABR decisions to the server
options.why: The server can't see the buffer, and per-viewer server logic breaks the caching model the whole design rests on.

items.q: Product wants a per-user visible watermark burned into every stream to deter piracy. What do you tell them?

options.t: Fine — it's just a filter in the encoder
options.why: The filter is easy; the consequence is not. Per-user pixels mean per-user files.

options.t: Unique bytes per viewer means the CDN hit rate goes to zero
options.why: Correct — this is the security-decision-with-cache-consequences moment. If you must, watermark only the top rung for a small high-risk cohort.

options.t: It is impossible to combine with DRM, since the segments are encrypted before delivery
options.why: It's technically possible and some studios require it. The blocker is economics, not feasibility.

options.t: Do it at the edge instead
options.why: Watermarking at the edge means the edge is transcoding per viewer — the same cost problem, moved somewhere more expensive.

items.q: Overnight, you start re-encoding the back catalog into AV1. By morning, creators report uploads taking 3 hours to become playable. What went wrong and what's the fix?

options.t: AV1 is slower per job; switch the backfill to H.264
options.why: The codec isn't the bug. Any large backfill in the same pool would have starved new uploads the same way.

options.t: The autoscaler reacted too slowly overnight; raise the scaling ceiling and pre-warm capacity
options.why: More capacity delays the symptom. Without lanes, backfill will happily consume whatever ceiling you set.

options.t: They share one queue; split into priority lanes with a floor for uploads
options.why: Right. Backfill has no deadline, uploads do, and only a weighted scheduler with a floor keeps that true under load.

options.t: Run the backfill during business hours instead
options.why: Now you starve uploads at the busiest time. Timing is not isolation.

items.q: At kickoff, 5 million players start a live stream and then poll the manifest on the same cadence forever. What's the highest-value fix?

options.t: Cache the manifest at the edge briefly, and jitter client refreshes
options.why: Even a one-second TTL collapses a million requests into one per edge per second, and jitter breaks the lockstep.

options.t: Add more origin replicas
options.why: Scaling origin to absorb a herd you could have collapsed at the edge is paying full price for an avoidable problem.

options.t: Switch the whole event to WebRTC so there is no manifest polling happening at all
options.why: That trades a cacheable protocol for one that scales with relay servers — vastly more expensive for a one-way broadcast.

options.t: Increase segment length to 30 seconds
options.why: It reduces polling but puts viewers a minute behind live, which is unacceptable for sport.

items.q: A creator says their view count read 41,200 last night and 39,850 this morning, and is furious. What is the honest engineering explanation?

options.t: A shard failed over and lost writes
options.why: Possible in general, but you don't reach for data loss when a designed-in reconciliation explains it exactly.

options.t: The live counter is approximate; the nightly settle recomputed it
options.why: Correct, and the product fix is to label the fast number as provisional rather than pretend both are exact.

options.t: The CDN double-counted cached segment requests during the evening peak
options.why: Views come from player heartbeats, not segment fetches — counting cache hits would be wildly wrong in both directions.

options.t: Views expire after 24 hours
options.why: Nothing in the design expires counted views; totals only get corrected, never aged out.

items.q: You're designing video for a startup delivering 50 TB a day. A staff engineer suggests building ISP-embedded appliances 'because that's what Netflix does'. Your call?

options.t: Agree — owning delivery is always cheaper at scale, and it is what the biggest players do
options.why: 'At scale' is doing all the work in that sentence, and 50 TB/day isn't it. Copying a solution without its precondition is the classic buzzword failure.

options.t: Rent a commercial CDN: at 50 TB/day the bill is a few hundred dollars a day
options.why: Right — the number gates the decision. Say the threshold out loud too: revisit when egress spend rivals a team plus hardware, not before.

options.t: Build a hybrid: half rented, half owned
options.why: You'd take on the entire operational burden of the owned half for a bill that isn't hurting yet. Hedging isn't judgment.

options.t: Defer the decision until traffic grows
options.why: Deferring without committing to today's choice or naming the trigger is exactly the option-listing that reads junior.

items.q: Ten minutes into 'design YouTube', you have a complete diagram. Where do you spend the remaining time to read as senior?

options.t: Detail the metadata schema, indexes, and channel-page queries
options.why: That's the easy part done thoroughly, which is exactly the mid-level trap: complete, competent, and aimed at the wrong room.

options.t: The transcoding pipeline and the delivery economics
options.why: Yes — making bytes and moving bytes are the two hard parts, and announcing that agenda yourself is the senior signal.

options.t: Recommendations, since that's what users experience
options.why: It's a different system with its own interview. Scoping it out with a latency budget and a fallback is the correct 20 seconds.

options.t: Comments, moderation, and the notification fan-out
options.why: All real features, none of them why this question is asked. You'd finish having never touched the crux.

items.q: The interviewer asks what breaks first if traffic and uploads both go 10x. Which answer shows the most production judgment?

options.t: Storage — an exabyte a year becomes ten, so we would need a new storage and tiering strategy
options.why: Storage growth is linear, boring and budgeted for. Naming the least surprising component suggests you haven't operated one of these.

options.t: The CDN — hit rates fall as content volume grows
options.why: It's the opposite, and that's the interesting bit: the popular head doesn't grow with traffic, so hit rate improves as you scale.

options.t: The transcode farm's peak burst and the egress bill — and cache hit rate improves
options.why: Correct on both halves. Naming the counterintuitive improvement unprompted is what separates recall from having thought about the economics.

options.t: The metadata database, which will need sharding
options.why: A billion rows is small and sharding is a solved move here. Reaching for the database is the reflex from other problems, not this one.

items.q: 'Netflix tunes an encoding ladder per title and pre-positions content overnight. Why doesn't YouTube just do the same?'

options.t: YouTube's engineers optimize for upload latency rather than for playback quality
options.why: Both companies care about both. Framing it as a preference misses that the constraint is structural.

options.t: A curated catalog is finite and predictable; a UGC firehose is neither
options.why: Right. Netflix amortizes heavy analysis over a hundred million views and knows tomorrow's demand; YouTube's median upload gets a handful of views and its popular head moves hourly.

options.t: AV1 makes per-title optimization unnecessary
options.why: A better codec shifts the curve but doesn't remove per-content complexity variation, which is what per-title tuning exploits.

options.t: YouTube's CDN can't hold predicted content
options.why: Capacity isn't the blocker — predictability is. You can't pre-position what nobody can predict.

items.q: Your team has a new encoder configuration that measures 8% more efficient offline. How do you ship it?

options.t: Roll it out fleet-wide once the offline benchmarks and quality checks have all passed
options.why: Offline efficiency and viewer experience are different measurements, and you're betting every stream on them being the same.

options.t: Ship to one region first, then the rest a week later
options.why: Better, but region-by-region without a control group leaves you guessing whether a rebuffer change was the encoder or the region.

options.t: A/B it on a slice of playback traffic, judged on rebuffer ratio
options.why: Right — '8% more efficient' and 'viewers stall more' are entirely compatible statements, so the user metric decides.

options.t: Ship it only for new uploads, so nothing existing changes
options.why: Safer on blast radius, but you still learn nothing measurable until you compare against a control on real playback.

items.q: Finance points out that mezzanine files are 20% of your storage bill and are 'never served to anyone'. A teammate proposes deleting them for videos older than a year. What do you say?

options.t: Agree, but keep mezzanines for videos above a view threshold and cold-store the rest
options.why: Closer, and tempting — but popularity can return years later, and a codec migration needs the whole catalog, not just today's head.

options.t: Refuse — the mezzanine is the source every future re-encode reads from
options.why: Correct. Renditions are derived data; the master is not. Move it to cold storage — that captures most of the saving without the one-way door.

options.t: Agree — renditions can always be re-encoded from the highest rung
options.why: Re-encoding from a lossy rendition compounds artifacts. Generation loss is real, and you can't undo it later.

options.t: Agree, and rely on CDN copies as backup
options.why: Caches are disposable by definition, hold only renditions, and evict the long tail first — exactly the content this would affect.

items.q: A live auction product demands sub-second end-to-end latency for 5 million concurrent viewers. What's the senior response?

options.t: Ship LL-HLS at 2 seconds and tell them it's close enough
options.why: Quietly missing a stated requirement isn't a trade-off, it's a surprise for someone else to discover in production.

options.t: Use WebRTC for everything and scale the relay tier up to five million viewers
options.why: Technically it works, and it puts every passive viewer on a cost curve that scales linearly with audience. You'd be paying real-time prices for one-way video.

options.t: Bid state over a persistent connection; video on LL-HLS at 2-3 s
options.why: Right. Sub-second is genuinely needed for a few hundred bytes of bid state, not for pixels — and naming the two-stack operational cost keeps it honest.

options.t: Refuse the requirement as technically impossible
options.why: It isn't impossible, it's expensive. Pushing back with numbers and a cheaper alternative beats refusing.
